paragraphs.heading: The Atlantic's main current system
paragraphs.text: The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, or AMOC, is the main system of ocean currents in the Atlantic. It is a major part of Earth's ocean circulation and has an important role in the climate system of the planet. Its currents make up half of the global thermohaline circulation, and the other half is the Southern Ocean overturning circulation. That global circulation links the world's oceans in a single "conveyor belt" of continuous water exchange.

paragraphs.heading: How the water moves
paragraphs.text: The AMOC includes currents at the surface and at great depths. Warm, saltier water flows north in the Atlantic's upper layers, and cold, less salty deep water flows back south. The warm water from the south is saltier because evaporation is higher in the tropical zone. When this upper layer cools, the salty water grows denser and sinks into the deep. Differences in temperature and salinity together drive the thermohaline circulation.

paragraphs.heading: Why the Atlantic is salty
paragraphs.text: The Pacific is less salty than the other oceans because it receives large amounts of fresh rain. Its surface water is not salty enough to sink below several hundred metres. North Atlantic water is saltier, partly because heavy evaporation concentrates salt in the water left behind and partly because sea ice near the Arctic Circle pushes out salt as it freezes in winter. Even more important, moisture that evaporates from the Atlantic is quickly carried away before it can fall back as rain. Trade winds take it across Central America to the eastern North Pacific, and there it comes down as rain. Atlantic surface water ends up salty and dense, and eventually sinks to form the North Atlantic Deep Water.

paragraphs.heading: The return trip
paragraphs.text: North Atlantic Deep Water forms mainly in the Nordic Seas. The downwelling that forms it is balanced by an equal amount of upwelling. The deep water moves south, and at the southern end of the Atlantic around 80% of it upwells in the Southern Ocean. That connects it with the Southern Ocean overturning circulation.

paragraphs.heading: Signs of weakening
paragraphs.text: Changes in the AMOC's strength can affect several parts of the climate system. Climate change may be weakening it through a rise in ocean heat content and larger flows of fresh water from melting Greenland ice sheets. Studies using oceanographic reconstructions suggest that as of 2015 it was weaker than before the Industrial Revolution. It is unclear how much of this weakening comes from climate change and how much from the circulation's natural variability over millennia. Climate models predict further weakening during the 21st century.

paragraphs.heading: What a weaker AMOC would do
paragraphs.text: The North Atlantic Current warms Scandinavia, Great Britain and Ireland, so a weaker AMOC would lower the average air temperatures over them. Around North America it would also speed up sea level rise, and in the North Atlantic it would reduce primary production. If the weakening is severe, the circulation may collapse, and that would not be reversible. That would make it one of the tipping points in the climate system. A collapse would substantially lower Europe's average temperature and its amount of rain and snowfall.
